articles.title: Meet Ava Grace Cummings, the 18-year-old North Carolina student who modelled STAC3 disorder, a rare hereditary muscle disease first identified in the Lumbee Tribe, in fruit flies and won $175,000 from Regeneron
articles.summary: US News: Ava Grace Cummings, an 18-year-old from North Carolina, wins $175,000 in the Regeneron Science Talent Search for her groundbreaking research on STAC3 disorder, a rare muscle disease in the Lumbee tribe, using fruit flies for potential new therapies.
articles.body: The Regeneron Science Talent Search is described by the Society for Science as the nation's oldest and most prestigious science and maths competition for high school seniors. It makes sense that most projects address issues that are somewhat unrelated to the researcher's personal life. Ava Grace Cummings made the opposite decision. The senior from Smithfield, North Carolina, who is eighteen years old, based her research on an illness she had personally witnessed in the faces of people she knew.Cummings, a member of the Lumbee and Coharie tribes, won second place and $175,000 in the 2025 competition for a study that used laboratory fruit flies to model STAC3 disorder, a rare genetic muscular condition. The flies were then used to test alternative therapies, including one based on traditional Indigenous herbal medicine.A sickness deeply ingrained in her own cultureFormerly known as Native American myopathy, STAC3 disorder is a congenital ailment that lowers muscle tone from birth and can cause joint stiffness, a cleft palate, a bent spine, and a potentially fatal reaction to some anaesthetic medications. It was initially identified in babies from the Lumbee tribe of North Carolina in the late 1980s, and it was subsequently linked to a single genetic mutation that was inherited among the group. GeneReviews estimates that STAC3 disorder affects about one in 5,000 Lumbee Native Americans. The condition has also been identified in other populations, including patients in southern Africa.For Cummings, STAC3 disorder was never an abstract condition. She told the Society for Science that seeing friends and family in the Lumbee Tribe struggle with the disease motivated her to raise awareness and look for potential treatments. There is no cure for STAC3 disorder, making the search for possible therapies an important part of her project.Turning fruit flies into a model of disease in actionTo study the rare muscle condition without human patients, Cummings turned to Drosophila. The fruit fly is widely used in genetics research because its short life cycle makes it possible to alter genes and observe changes over a relatively short period. Cummings created a strain of flies that did not express the dstac gene, the fly counterpart of the gene disrupted in STAC3 disorder. The resulting flies showed muscle-weakness traits that allowed her to model the condition in the laboratory.Armed with a workable model, she investigated two prospective therapies. One was Tirasemtiv, an experimental drug being studied for its effects on muscle contraction and neuromuscular function. The other was stinging nettle, Urtica dioica, a plant that many traditional herbal medicines employed, some of which her tribe used. She tested affected adult flies by measuring how well they climbed the walls of a test vial, while the larvae were assessed by the distance they travelled. Flies treated with nettle extract alone climbed better, while the larvae also travelled farther than untreated groups. The combination of nettle extract and Tirasemtiv produced the strongest improvement among the treatments tested.Connecting Two Medical SystemsRather than seeing Indigenous medicine and pharmaceutical research as two separate worlds, Cummings considers her study an attempt to bring the two into parity. She has said she hopes her study will bring greater attention, funding and therapeutic interest to illnesses that impact small, unique populations and are otherwise easily overlooked by the broader medical research system.During high school, she attended the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics in Durham, where she founded and led the school's Natives Rising chapter. She also plays the piano, is a member of her school soccer team and serves as a resident life advisor. Cummings' second-place finish was also part of a notable milestone for the competition. Alongside fourth-place winner Logan Lee, a Native Hawaiian student, she was one of two Indigenous students to receive a top-10 prize in the 2025 Regeneron Science Talent Search. Native America Calling reported that it was the first time two Indigenous students had received top-10 awards in the competition's 83-year history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the late 20th century, American soybean seeds arrived in China to increase yields, but contaminated shipments introduced invasive weeds that spread across thousands of fields
articles.summary: US News: Discover how contaminated soybean shipments from the US introduced invasive weeds such as Palmer Amaranth into China, impacting agriculture and prompting biosecurity measures.
articles.body: Soybean imports from the United States have carried seeds of foreign plants into Chinese ports, with some of those weeds later establishing populations beyond the places where they were first detected. One of the clearest examples is Palmer amaranth (Amaranthus palmeri), a weed that is native to the Americas and has become an agricultural problem in parts of China. A 2026 study in the Journal of Integrative Agriculture traced populations of the weed in China and found evidence that linked repeated introductions to imported soybean shipments.The research identified 1985 as the date of an initial introduction in Beijing and found that later populations were associated with the movement of imported soybeans. The researchers concluded that repeated introductions through global grain trade played a major role in the weed's distribution across China.The pathway ran through imported grainWeed seeds can become mixed with harvested grain as crops are collected, stored and transported, and some seeds can survive the journey and enter agricultural areas if they are not detected or removed. Chinese officials raised concerns about this pathway directly with U.S. authorities in 2017, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said China had notified the agency about increased detections of weed seeds of quarantine concern in U.S. soybean shipments.USDA subsequently developed a farm-to-export systems approach that was intended to reduce the amount of foreign material and weed seed entering soybean consignments, which was scheduled to begin with the 2018 crop year.The issue was important enough to affect the phytosanitary conditions under which U.S. soybeans could enter the Chinese market. USDA said the measures were designed to reduce plant-pest risk while keeping soybean exports moving.Palmer amaranth spread beyond its first arrival pointsA 2025 study published through the National Library of Medicine reported that Amaranthus palmeri seeds had been repeatedly introduced into China as contaminants in soybean imports since 1985. The researchers found that populations were concentrated near grain-import facilities and documented cases in southern, central, northern and northeastern China.Grain facilities provide a starting point, after which seeds can move through agricultural machinery, transportation networks and crop production areas. The researchers also found that populations differed in their degree of establishment; some remained temporary, while others became naturalized or invasive and spread beyond their initial locations.Palmer amaranth is particularly difficult to manage because individual plants can produce large quantities of seed and the weed can compete aggressively with crops. Its presence in China therefore became more than a matter of contaminated cargo, and it eventually became a question of whether a plant introduced through international trade could establish itself in agricultural landscapes.Biosecurity became part of the soybean tradeSoybeans are traded in bulk, and separating every foreign seed from a large shipment is difficult, so prevention has to begin before the grain reaches a port. USDA's 2018 systems approach included measures at farms, export facilities and other points in the supply chain, with the goal being to reduce the number of weed seeds entering them in the first place.The practical problem is that once a species establishes itself in a new agricultural region, removing it can be much harder than preventing the original introduction. The newer research on A. palmeri suggests that the trade route remains important, as its analysis found genetic and geographic patterns that were consistent with repeated introductions linked to soybean imports, rather than a single introduction followed by uninterrupted expansion.The original soybean shipments were part of a much larger trade system moving food and animal feed across continents, but within those cargoes, tiny quantities of weed seed could travel the same routes. In China's fields, some of those seeds found conditions in which they could establish and spread.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Bandar Utama stabbing: Malaysian boy acquitted for murder of schoolgirl on grounds of insanity
articles.summary: The killing of the 16-year-old nearly a year ago had shocked Malaysia and sparked debate about social media.
articles.body:
A Malaysian teenage boy charged with the high-profile murder of a female schoolmate has been acquitted, with the judge finding the boy was mentally unsound during the incident.

He had fatally stabbed Yap Shing Xuen in a toilet at their secondary school on the outskirts of the capital Kuala Lumpur.

The killing of the 16-year-old girl had shocked Malaysia and sparked debate about the effects of social media on children.

Police previously had said they suspected social media could have influenced the boy, who was 14 at the time. The case was seen to have spurred authorities to limit children's access to social media, which began earlier this year.

The boy - who cannot be named under Malaysian law as he is still a minor - had pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.

During the trial defence lawyers did not deny that the boy killed the girl, but argued that he had suffered from poor mental health for years and asked for his acquittal on the grounds of insanity.

An expert witness, a psychiatrist, testified that the boy had schizophrenia, and had suffered from mental illness and experienced delusions since he was nine years old.

The boy's condition was said to have worsened during the pandemic and when he eventually returned to school. Lawyers had said that the boy would need medication for the rest of his life to manage symptoms.

On Monday the judge ruled that the boy would be acquitted, but also ordered for him to be detained and to receive treatment at a psychiatric hospital.

He will stay at the hospital until he is deemed fit to be released back to society, and would likely be subject to yearly assessments.

A defence lawyer told reporters on Monday that upon hearing the verdict, the boy appeared "neutral in emotion, but he understands what is going on, [that] it's a very serious matter".

The trial and verdict hearings were held in a closed court, which meant that the public and media could not attend.

Malaysian boy on trial for allegedly murdering girl in school

The case has profoundly shocked Malaysia and sparked a nationwide conversation about the negative effects of social media on children.

Much of this conversation was triggered by the contents of a note that police had found on the boy at the time of his arrest, which was leaked online and widely circulated.

Some people had compared the case to the Netflix series Adolescence, which featured a storyline about a young boy killing a female schoolmate and explored the theme of online radicalisation.

Last year, the country's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was asked about the case as well as other recent cases of violence in schools.

He was quoted by local media as saying that "almost all of these issues stem from the use of mobile phones and social media", and vowed to look into stricter measures.

Authorities have since put in place new rules which they say will protect children and reduce their exposure to harmful online content.

Since June, Malaysia has banned all children under the age of 16 from having accounts on major social media platforms.

articles.title: 'Spoils of war': Iran says US submarine seized in Hormuz was 'captured, not confiscated'
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei on Monday said the American submarine seized by Iran was “captured as spoils of war”, adding that.
articles.body: Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei on Monday said the American submarine seized by Iran was “captured as spoils of war”, adding that such spoils are legitimate."It was not confiscated; it was captured as spoils of war, and such spoils are legitimate," Baghaei said, as reported by Iran’s IRNA News Agency.On Saudi Arabia’s request to postpone the regional summit, Baghaei said attributing the move to developments in Yemen was a deviation from the main roots of the crisis.Baghaei added that Iran has consistently supported the roadmap agreed upon by the Yemeni parties and said the continuation of conflict among Islamic countries served the "Zionist regime's goals for perpetuating insecurity"."Iran has always supported the roadmap agreed upon by the Yemeni parties and considers the continuation of conflict between Islamic countries to be in line with the Zionist regime's goals for perpetuating insecurity," he said.Earlier last week, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said that it had captured a US unmanned underwater vehicle near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, describing it as one of the most advanced systems operated by the US military.In a statement published by Sepah media, the IRGC described the unmanned submarine as the "most modern, smart" unmanned submarine device. Iranian state media identified the vehicle as the Dive-LD, an autonomous underwater vehicle manufactured by California-based defence technology company Anduril Industries.The IRGC Navy said it had intercepted the submarine at the entrance to the strategically important strait and described it as a “prize” now in Iranian possession.This comes as the conflict in West Asia shows signs of renewed escalation, with fighting intensifying in Yemen as Houthi rebels advance towards Saudi-backed government-held areas, including the strategic oil- and gas-rich province of Marib and the city of Taiz, putting growing pressure on Saudi Arabia to respond.The Houthi advance towards government strongholds in Marib and Taiz has raised concerns over a renewed offensive. Marib has remained one of Yemen's most strategically important government-held areas since the conflict escalated in 2015, hosting major army bases, oil and gas fields, a key power station and more than two million displaced people, as reported by Al Jazeera.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Parents among 4 shot dead, kid battles bullet injuries: How violence struck 2 Manipur villages on ‘Black Day’
articles.summary: IMPHAL: A six-year-old boy is battling bullet injuries after his parents were shot dead in a pre-dawn attack in Manipur’s Tamenglong district, while t.
articles.body: IMPHAL: A six-year-old boy is battling bullet injuries after his parents were shot dead in a pre-dawn attack in Manipur’s Tamenglong district, while two other people were killed in a separate attack in neighbouring Noney district on Sunday, in a bloody day for Kuki villages observed as ‘Black Day’ by the community.In the first attack, unidentified gunmen opened fire at L Tollen village in Tamenglong around 4am, killing 42-year-old Lhingjangai Singsit. Her husband, 54-year-old Seikhoneh Singsit, and their six-year-old son were also shot.Seikhoneh initially survived the attack but later succumbed to his injuries in hospital, leaving the child injured after the attack that claimed both his parents.Hours later, at around 3pm, another attack took place in Longpi village in Noney district. Julie Singson and Roel Gangte, both in their 30s, were killed while reportedly collecting essential household items. Julie was reportedly pregnant.Another woman who was with the group is reportedly missing and is feared to have been abducted. Both victims were residents of Longpi village.The two attacks took place on a day observed by the Kuki community as ‘Black Day’ to commemorate those killed and displaced during the violence of the 1990s.The L Tollen village authority alleged that cadres of the NSCN (IM) and ZUF (K) were behind the attack.“While we are still bearing the deep scars of the 1993 ethnic persecution of the Kuki people under the leadership of NSCN (IM), this inhumane act has once again opened our old wounds,” it said.“This is not an isolated incident. It is a systematic and deliberate attempt to terrorize, uproot, and ethnically cleanse the Kuki-Zo villagers from our ancestral lands to fulfill their Greater Nagalim agenda. The L Tollen village authority considers this act as a blatant act of terrorism against innocent civilians and a grave violation of human rights,” the organisation said.It demanded the deployment of adequate central forces in L Tollen and adjoining Kuki villages and the arrest of those responsible.The office of the western village volunteers, Jiribam, Tamenglong and Noney, also alleged that NSCN (IM) and ZUF-K cadres carried out the Longpi attack. It said the attackers advanced towards the village centre but were driven back after an exchange of fire with the volunteers.The Kuki Inpi Jiri, Tamenglong and Noney (JTN) has given the state government 24 hours to take concrete action and announced a 24-hour economic blockade. It warned that an indefinite shutdown would follow if its demands were not met.The organisation also expressed concern that the L Tollen attack took place only a few hundred metres from a CSF deployment.Chief minister Y Khemchand Singh expressed deep anguish over the killings, saying that violence against innocent civilians is a cowardly act and unacceptable.The ethnic conflict that erupted in May 2023 between the valley-based Meitei and the hill-based Kuki communities has claimed at least 306 lives, with 49 individuals remaining missing and thousands left homeless.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Imphal news. articles.title: In 2008, an Australian couple bought coastal land and found a pristine 'unicorn' aquifer; 18 years later, they are selling it as fine water for $10 a bottle, after it scored 100/100
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Damien Smith, a passionate South Australian surfer, and his wife, Gretchen Scinta, moved to the western coast of Yorke Peninsula to catch the waves. W.
articles.body: Damien Smith, a passionate South Australian surfer, and his wife, Gretchen Scinta, moved to the western coast of Yorke Peninsula to catch the waves. What they really caught was something even more precious: fresh water that’s worth bottling. Soon, the land turned them into fine-water producers, with their bottled water earning a perfect 100-point score, ABC News reported.The couple bought the Yorke Peninsula property in 2008, and a few years later, they noticed something extraordinary. They noticed crayfish thriving in the back paddock. This was strange given that crayfish are freshwater dwellers, and the land they bought is surrounded by ocean. They consulted an engineer and discovered that their land was a geological anomaly. They were sitting on an isolated underground aquifer so pristine that it barely needed extraction or processing. The water had never been touched by contamination. It's naturally mineralised. And that’s how the ocean-loving couple tapped into the growing global fine-water market. Their water is now served at Adelaide's 2KW, bysommelier Dan McEvoy for $10 a bottle.They hit a ‘unicorn’All of it began with an accidental discovery. The couple came for the ocean and waves, but stumbled upon something else. "I'd been surfing this coast for over 35 years now. 20 years ago I came back with Gretchen, she fell in love with this remote stretch of South Australia's Yorke Peninsula. We came for the surf, the coastline and the lifestyle. What we discovered beneath the dunes was something extraordinary — a naturally mineralised aquifer that would eventually become Carribie Mineral Water," the couple said in a post shared on Instagram.And the discovery really started from the crayfish they saw in the paddock. They wondered how freshwater crayfish could survive on land surrounded by ocean. "The tip for us was [the] freshwater crayfish down in the back paddock, but you're so close to the ocean, so you're starting to go, what's going on here?" Smith told the broadcaster. They used this water for their house and to grow vegetables. They were curious enough to test the water, only to discover that they were sitting on something special. “This is a unicorn,” a water engineer told them. "He said it's the balance of the minerals in it, but it's pristine because it's so isolated, so no-one's touched this water,” Smith recalled.Water so pristine that it could be savoured like wineDamien Smith and his wife, Gretchen Scinta, had worked in the wine industry for years. So when they discovered an underground aquifer on their land, they knew what they had to do. They bottled it and built their brand, Carribie, which sells mineral water sourced from their land on the Yorke Peninsula, overlooking the Great Southern Ocean. The water scored a perfect 100 from judges at an international fine-water tasting. The sparkling version came close behind at 99. A 12-bottle case of still mineral water now sells for $69, with the sparkling water priced at the same rate, according to their website.The fine-water market may sound niche, but the industry is growing with demand for pristine water. And its producers are challenging the idea of water as a commodity. One among them is food anthropologist Michael Mascha, who co-founded the Fine Water Society after his heart forced him to quit alcohol. He argues that water has terroir like wine and can be matched with food. The movement is gaining momentum, especially as the global population is slowly turning away from alcoholic beverages. "I looked around the table, and there was another bottle there, which was water," Mascha said. Though premium water initially didn’t get attention, people have started to take it seriously. “Salt has made a transition from a commodity to a product with terroir, olive oil, chocolate, other products like this, and I think water is now in the process of making exactly the same transition.”Australia arrived early to this market and is finding its footing. "Australia is definitely a brand that started very early, then there was a little bit of a lull, but I see now Australia is a country that's really up and coming,” he said.The source mattersSmith and Scinta's mineral water is in demand because of the source. They've resisted the industrial logic that treats water extraction as a simple commodity play. The aquifer exists in the Carribie Basin, accessed through a sealed point that minimises contact with the surface. They move the water through food-grade pipes underground into holding tanks, limiting oxygen, light and temperature changes, without any treatments or shortcuts. According to Smith, that's all it needs: "The important thing here is, limit oxygen, limit light, and limit changes in temperature … so we do literally do nothing."This hands-off approach runs counter to how most premium waters reach the market, especially after the recent scandals that exposed what happens when scale prioritises cost-cutting. In 2024, Nestlé Waters admitted using banned filters and ultraviolet treatment on mineral waters, paying a €2-million fine to avoid legal action. The reputational damage rippled through the entire bottled-water industry, sharpening consumer scrutiny about sourcing and processing methods.Amid the rising demand, Gretchen Scinta is training to become a certified water sommelier. This is perhaps a credential that wouldn't have made sense a decade ago. But now it does. Australian restaurants are starting to treat water with the care once reserved for wine pairings. Now the question really is: Would you pay hundreds of dollars for fine water?Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘I was scared and angry’: Bill Clinton reveals CIA abandoned pre-9/11 plan to take out Bin Laden
articles.summary: US News: In a recent interview, former President Bill Clinton revealed that the CIA abandoned a critical pre-9/11 operation to eliminate Osama Bin Laden due to concerns about potential civilian casualties. Clinton shared his feelings of anger and fear over this decision while discussing the implications and lessons learned since the September 11 attacks.
articles.body: Former US President Bill Clinton has revealed that the CIA abandoned a plan to take out Osama bin Laden before the September 11 attacks because officials feared civilians could be killed if the operation failed.Speaking on WABC's “Cats Roundtable” with host John Catsimatidis on Sunday, Clinton said he had authorised the CIA to target the al Qaeda leader and would have preferred to see him captured alive, although stopping him was the priority.Clinton said he was “scared” and angry when the agency called off the operation, which he believed could have succeeded.“But they were afraid that if they missed, they’d kill a lot of innocent civilians,” Clinton said. “They didn’t want to run the risk.”He added that he did not second-guess the agency's decision, but believed bin Laden had the resources and determination to attack the US.Clinton also recalled the moment he realised bin Laden was likely responsible for the September 11 attacks. He was in Australia when the second plane struck the World Trade Centre, while his wife Hillary Clinton was in Washington and their daughter was in Lower Manhattan.Clinton said his family was unable to reach their daughter as people in the area were instructed to leave and walk north.“I was watching television in Australia when the second plane hit. I immediately said that bin Laden did this,” Clinton recalled.He said bin Laden was among the few US adversaries he believed had both the motive and capability to carry out such an attack, adding that the al Qaeda leader had been planning an assault on American soil for years.Bin Laden was eventually killed on May 2, 2011, during a US Navy SEAL raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan. The operation was authorised by then-President Barack Obama.Clinton also warned that New York City could face another terrorist attack, although he said the US is now better prepared than it was before 9/11.“I think it’s entirely possible. I think we have to stay on guard about that,” Clinton said, stressing the need for continued intelligence gathering.“We’re much better prepared [now] than we were,” he said, while warning that a single intelligence failure could have serious consequences.Clinton said preventing major threats while delivering positive results should remain a priority for the US and could help bring greater unity to the country.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: More than a summer home: A look inside the Kennedys' historic Hyannis Port estate
articles.summary: News News: For nearly a century, the Kennedy family’s sprawling compound in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, has been more than a summer retreat.Set along the waterf.
articles.body: For nearly a century, the Kennedy family’s sprawling compound in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, has been more than a summer retreat.Set along the waterfront of Cape Cod, the property has hosted generations of Kennedys, witnessed key moments in American political history and offered the family a private place to celebrate, compete and grieve, the New York Post reported.The compound’s lawns and private pier became familiar backdrops to images of the family sailing on Nantucket Sound, swimming off the Cape Cod coast and playing fiercely competitive games of touch football. Those photographs helped shape the idyllic “Camelot” image associated with the Kennedy dynasty.As summer draws to a close, the historic property once again offers a glimpse into the family’s private world—and the real estate that has remained closely linked to its public legacy.How the Kennedys found Hyannis PortThe family’s connection to Hyannis Port began with golf. In 1926, Joseph P Kennedy, already a millionaire, began looking for a home near a golf club. He reportedly explored membership at Cohasset Country Club on Massachusetts’ South Shore but was turned away, allegedly because of his Irish Catholic faith, the Post reported.The Kennedys later discovered Hyannisport Club on Cape Cod, which was then run by an Irish Catholic. The family rented Malcolm Cottage before Joseph Kennedy purchased the property in 1928 for $25,000, according to the JFK Museum in Hyannis.The original three-acre property stood on a dead-end street facing Nantucket Sound. Over time, it grew into a multigenerational waterfront compound that became one of the most recognisable family estates in the United States.A waterfront estate built for family lifeJoseph Kennedy expanded the main residence, known as the Big House, into a sprawling home reportedly featuring 21 rooms, 12 bedrooms, a steam room and a 50-person theatre in the basement.The grounds included a tennis court, swimming pool and open lawns where the Kennedy children played touch football. The waterfront location also made sailing, swimming and boating central to family life.In 1956, John F. Kennedy purchased a house behind his father’s residence. It later became known as the President’s House. Robert F. Kennedy and his wife, Ethel, bought another adjacent property, creating the core of the compound that exists today, the realtor.com reported.Hyannis Port was not only a place for summer holidays. It also played a role in John F. Kennedy’s political career. It was at the main house that Kennedy reportedly decided to run for president in 1960. The property later served as his campaign headquarters.During Kennedy’s presidency, the compound became known as the “seaside White House”. He once reflected on the importance of the Cape Cod retreat, saying: “I always come back to the Cape and walk on the beach when I have a tough decision to make.”Photographs of Kennedy and his wife, Jacqueline, spending time with their children at the compound helped turn the property into a symbol of family life behind the White House.Kennedy spent his final Labor Day holiday at Hyannis Port from August 29 to September 2, 1963, less than three months before his assassination.Archival photographs and home-movie footage preserved by the John F Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum show the president enjoying a weekend filled with familiar family activities.After Kennedy’s death, Hyannis Port became closely associated with the memory of his presidency. It was also where Jacqueline Kennedy sought refuge after the assassination.In the aftermath, she helped shape the “Camelot” image of Kennedy’s White House, drawing on the late president’s fondness for the Broadway musical.In her first official interview after his death, she said: “Don’t let it be forgot, that for one brief, shining moment there was Camelot.”Over the years, the compound also became a place where the family gathered to mourn major losses, including the deaths of Joseph P Kennedy Jr during World War II, Robert F Kennedy in 1968 and John F Kennedy Jr, who died in a plane crash with his wife, Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, in 1999.The property was designated a US National Historic Landmark in 1972, reflecting its significance in American political and cultural history. Despite its association with tragedy and political history, Hyannis Port has remained a place for family celebrations.The Kennedy descendants continue to gather at the compound for an annual Fourth of July reunion. Family photographs once shared with the media are now frequently posted on social media, offering glimpses of the extended family gathering on the historic property.The compound is unlikely to enter the real estate market anytime soon. However, several nearby properties offer a taste of the waterfront lifestyle associated with Hyannis Port.A historic seaside estate on Washington Avenue is listed for $7,999,999. Built in 1920, the property includes 10 bedrooms, 6.5 bathrooms and about 5,500 square feet spread across a main house and guesthouse. It features water views, a built-in bar, three fireplaces, a covered porch, three garage bays and space for guests.For buyers seeking a more modest Cape Cod home, a three-bedroom beach house in Hyannis is listed for $899,900. The 1,800-square-foot property features marsh views, a gas fireplace, a private deck and a second-floor terrace.While these homes cannot replicate the history of the Kennedy compound, they offer a connection to the same coastal setting that has defined the family’s summers for generations.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Maharashtra govt aims to table UCC Bill in assembly winter session: CM Fadnavis
articles.summary: India News: The Maharashtra government plans to table its Uniform Civil Code (UCC) Bill during the winter session of the state assembly in Nagpur, chief minister .
articles.body: The Maharashtra government plans to table its Uniform Civil Code (UCC) Bill during the winter session of the state assembly in Nagpur, chief minister Devendra Fadnavis said on Monday. Fadnavis said the government will move ahead with the proposed legislation once the seven-member panel appointed to examine the UCC submits its report.Fadnavis confirmed on Monday that the committee headed by retired Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Desai is currently working on the framework for the proposed code and that the government would act after receiving its report."Look, the Maharashtra government has already formed a committee to prepare the Uniform Civil Code. The committee is working, and I believe that once the committee submits its report, we will implement it soon," he told reporters.The chief minister also reiterated that the government would proceed with implementation after the panel completes its exercise."The Maharashtra government has constituted a committee on UCC, and it is working on the matter. We will proceed with implementation as soon as the panel submits its report," Fadnavis said.The seven-member committee was set up in July with a six-month deadline to submit its recommendations. Its members include former high court judges R C Chavan and S G Mehare, former chief secretary D K Jain, former advocate general Virendra Saraf, constitutional expert Ramesh Patange and educationist Suvarna Rawal, apart from Justice Desai.Fadnavis' announcement came a day after Union home minister Amit Shah said BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states would introduce the UCC before 2029. Uttarakhand, Gujarat and Assam have already passed UCC legislation, in February 2024, March 2026 and May 2026 respectively.Separately, Fadnavis hit out at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over the political debate surrounding the vegetarian menu served at the BRICS Summit dinner in Delhi."BRICS was not organised for a dinner," Fadnavis said, arguing that the focus should instead remain on the summit's diplomatic outcome.He highlighted the unanimous adoption of the New Delhi Declaration, saying China, Russia and other participating countries had signed the document, which included a reference to terrorism and Pakistan."The New Delhi Declaration was unanimous. China and Russia signed it. Some people get stomach ache because of India's diplomatic victory, so they bring up issues like food and cultural programmes," he said.Fadnavis further said, "There could be no greater diplomatic or strategic victory for India than this. articles.title: Surrogate mother discovers baby’s father is Chinese billionaire with 300 US-born children who dreams of a Musk family match
articles.summary: US News: The American surrogate industry is currently in a roundabout, with its activities unravelling one by one. One surrogate in the country tried five time.
articles.body: The American surrogate industry is currently in a roundabout, with its activities unravelling one by one. One surrogate in the country tried five times to meet the intended father of the baby she was carrying, only to learn that he was Chinese billionaire and video game executive Xu Bo, who has been reported to have more than 100 children through US surrogacy arrangements, as per an IBT report.The woman, referred to as 'Judy' to protect her identity, was 12 weeks pregnant when CBS News informed her that documents identified Xu as the intended father. She had been told she was carrying a child for a single father who wanted a 'big family'. 'It leaves me wondering: do I even have a right to know?' Judy said after learning more about the intended father's reported family arrangements.The number of children Xu has is disputed, with his former partner Tang Jing alleging he could have as many as 300, while Xu says he has custody of 12 children born through surrogacy in US.An in-depth investigationJudy said she responded to a surrogacy advertisement because she hoped the arrangement would improve the financial conditions of her family and her seven-year-old daughter. The ad was posted on Instagram, offering $120,000 to become a surrogate. After being matched through Patriot Conceptions, she said she was told the intended parent was a single father. She said she asked how many other surrogates he had hired and was told the number was close to two dozen. She later learned that Xu was reportedly working with more than 20 other surrogates at the same time.Describing what she imagined when told the intended parent wanted a large family, Judy said she was 'picturing The Sound of Music'. She questioned whether women entering surrogacy agreements should be given more information about intended parents, including their other arrangements. “It leaves me wondering: do I even have a right to know?” she said.Despite her concerns, Judy said she felt obligated to continue because she had already signed the contract and needed the income. Friends and relatives also encouraged her to move ahead with the pregnancy.An image posted on a social media account linked to Xu showed more than 100 young children seated in rows. A statement in Chinese attributed to him said that 'more children bring more blessings' and that he wanted his actions to contribute to China's long-term development.Not just fathering children, Xu reportedly hopes his kids will one day marry Elon Musk's children and create a sprawling family dynasty, as per an NYP report.A fatherly dream?Xu Bo is a 48-year-old wealthy recluse who founded the online gaming company Duoyi and calls himself "China's first father." He has been bent on siring at least "50 high-quality sons," according to social media posts verified as his by WSJ.Xu’s quest to build a family dynasty was reportedly inspired by Musk, who has been rumoured to offer friends and family sperm in an effort to build his bloodline, claims that the Tesla titan has denied. On Weibo, Xu has posted fantasies of his offspring one day marrying Musk’s children, according to the Journal.In the summer of 2023, a judge in California handled petitions from Xu to gain parental rights for four unborn children, as well as at least eight other children who he paid for through surrogates. The judge immediately called a confidential hearing, and Xu appeared over video.The billionaire told the judge he hoped to sire 20 or more U.S.-born children, boys specifically because they are superior, to one day take over his business. Many of his children have reportedly lived in a home in Irvine, Calif., and been raised by nannies.Xu told the judge he hadn’t met them yet because work had been busy but said he planned to bring them to China soon. The judge rejected his petition for parental rights, leaving the unborn children in legal limbo and exposing an insane industry of surrogacy companies helping wealthy Chinese businessmen have American-born children, the Journal reported.American surrogate industry in spotlightA wider investigation involved interviews with 32 surrogates and a review of contracts and court documents. It found examples of intended parents using several surrogates simultaneously, with some women saying they were not told about the scale of those arrangements.Sperm banks in the United States sometimes use one donor’s sperm to father children at a similar rate to Xu. An Atlanta man who donated his sperm as a student at Georgia State University in 2011 was shocked to find out years later that he was the biological father of at least 97 children.The incident with Xu has now raised questions about disclosure requirements in the American surrogate industry. Attorney Melissa Brisman, who has represented surrogates and intended parents, told the investigation that there are no laws governing how many surrogates one set of intended parents can use simultaneously.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Local election candidates told to respect each other as abuse rises
articles.summary: A survey suggests more than half of candidates in the May 2026 polls in England faced harassment or intimidation.
articles.body:
Political parties should require members to respect one another during elections, the Electoral Commission has said after finding rising levels of abuse.

More than half of candidates in the May 2026 English local and mayoral polls experienced a problem with harassment or intimidation, the highest level over the last four years, according to its survey of 25,000 who stood.

A report published on Monday said such issues were most likely to affect women, people from ethnic minority backgrounds and those with a disability.

The watchdog is calling on political parties to make clear in their own rules that members "must respect other campaigners", with potential disciplinary action if they do not.

The report also recommended requiring social media companies to improve protections for electoral candidates online, including rapidly removing abusive content and identifying perpetrators.

Inappropriate contact through social media was the most frequently experienced scenario of harassment or abuse for local candidates, the survey found, with disinformation through generative AI also flagged as an issue.

One candidate told the survey their daughter had "called me from school crying" because she had seen posts online branding them "racist, fascist and Nazi".

Another candidate reported being screamed at with death threats while leafleting on doorsteps, but could not run away because of their disability.

Reform UK and Labour candidates were more than twice as likely as Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to say they had experienced such issues in the May 2026 elections in England , with the Greens and independents between both groups.

Some 79% of female respondents reported avoiding the campaign trail on their own at least once, compared to just under half of male counterparts. One female candidate said they felt the need to bring their husband with them.

And a third of respondents overall considered not standing for election because of harassment, intimidation or concerns about future abuse.

Only 15% of those surveyed had reported such experiences to the police.

"These elections demonstrate the growing threats posed to democracy," the Electoral Commission's chief executive Vijay Rangarajan said.

He added: "Without improvements to candidate safety, there is a significant risk that people will be put off standing in future elections."

articles.title: Ex-CIA boss was at Ukrainian station when Russian drone struck train
articles.summary: Former US CIA director David Petraeus was at a Ukrainian train station at the very moment a Russian drone struck a passenger train on Sunday, shortly after a...
articles.body:
Former US CIA director David Petraeus was at a Ukrainian train station at the very moment a Russian drone struck a passenger train on Sunday, shortly after a diplomatic train carrying former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other foreign dignitaries had passed through.

Kyiv framed the attack as evidence of the increased threat Russia's Vladimir Putin poses to Europe, with Ukraine's rail operator saying it was "quite likely" a targeted attack.

The diplomatic train carrying Johnson, European security officials and other former leaders from Kyiv to Poland had made an early departure from Yahodyn station –– about two kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border –– due to the "constant threat of Russian strikes," said Ukrainian Railways. It had already crossed into Poland by the time of the attack.

Petraeus was traveling on a separate train which was still at Yahodyn station, a Ukrainian Railways statement said. CNN has reached out to Petraeus for comment.

The rail operator said that while it was still clarifying details, it is "quite likely" that the Russian drone could have deliberately targeted the officials' train.

Russian drones also targeted a gas station in the same town on Sunday.

"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO," said Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, in a message condemning to Russian attacks on the Yahodyn border crossing point.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces were targeting "railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that are used to transport military cargoes from European countries," according to state news agency TASS.

Johnson, the former British leader who has continued to be a vocal advocate Ukraine, condemned the Russian attack, saying he didn't know "what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive," in a post to X.

"What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day – even on civilian railways."

The former prime minister of Sweden, Carl Bildt, was also on a train near the Polish border at the time.

"This wasn't our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing," Bildt wrote on X alongside a video appearing to show a drone hitting a nearby train as throngs of passengers evacuate.

Petraeus and the European officials had been attending an international security conference in Kyiv known as the Yalta European Strategy (YES).

Russia escalates attacks near Polish border

Russia has stepped up its attacks near the Polish border in recent weeks, including in Yahodyn, which is a major pathway for Western military and humanitarian aid into Ukraine. Earlier Sunday, Russia struck a gas station in the border town, briefly shutting the crossing.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, speaking in Kyiv on Sunday, warned of the wider implications of Russian attacks close to Poland's border.

"This is an escalation. It is another major challenge for Ukraine, but also for the potential future victims of Russian aggression," Sikorski said.

Late Sunday night, British Defense Minister Wes Streeting said Russian attacks near the border, including on the gas facility, served as a "stark reminder" of what Ukrainians face everyday.

"Reckless, dangerous attacks on civilian infrastructure so close to Poland also underline the wider security threat Russia poses," he said, adding the UK would continue to work with allies to bolster European security.

The train attack comes less than one week after a Russian drone entered Moldovan airspace as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was about to take off from an airport in the country's capital. Moldova is not a NATO state but has a longstanding partnership with the North Atlantic military alliance.

articles.title: Romanian driver who killed triathlete Rebecca Comins to be deported
articles.summary: Romanian van driver Visile Barbu's appeal against deportation was dismissed by a judge.
articles.body:
A Romanian van driver jailed for killing a Team GB triathlete by driving into the back of her bike has lost an appeal against being deported.

Visile Barbu, 50 was delivering furniture to a driver in Calais when he hit Rebecca Comins' bike in June 2022.

Barbu drove straight into the back of Comins rather than move into an empty lane of the dual carriageway. He was was found guilty of causing her death by dangerous driving following a five day trial .

At the hearing in Newport, immigration judge Ian Boyes said: "The nature of the offending is important. This was not an accident. It was not a slight misjudgement. It was committed using a vehicle which should not have been on the road."

Comins, 52, was nine minutes into a cycling time trial on the A40 near Raglan, Monmouthshire, when Barbu tried to overtake.

He said he had seen her, but did not know why he hit her, claiming he would ask himself the question for his "whole life".

When his van was examined following the crash it was found to be unfit for the road and its load overweight which would have increased the emergency breaking distances and ability to turn the wheel, according to a vehicle examiner.

Barbu moved to Britain in 2002 to become a pub chef at Old Pandy public house and eventually owned the pub. Barbu married a Romanian woman, Maria, in 2004 and had twins, who are now adults.

He filed an appeal to stop him from being deported, and said it would be "unduly harsh for both him and his family to relocate permanently to Romania, where he said he has no home or source of income.

He said he identified closely with British culture and traditions and regarded the UK as his permanent home.

His wife Maria said she would not relocate to Romania, and would be unable to cope without her husband.

On 7 September, Boyes said as Barbu's children were adults and do not depend on him, it would not be "unduly harsh" to remove him.

He said "the very significant public interest in deportation outweighs the appellant's private and family life considerations."

articles.title: Munir fails Mecca test: Why Pakistan’s Field Marshal is not riding to rescue MBS
articles.summary: Pakistan News: As Houthi forces seized Mokha and Perim Island last week, Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spent the moment on the phone with Iran's for.
articles.body: As Houthi forces seized Mokha and Perim Island last week, Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spent the moment on the phone with Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi.Munir seems in no hurry to mobilise Pakistan military against Saudi Arabia's attackers.Why it matters: Saudi Arabia’s Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) planned the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Turkey specifically as insurance against a moment like this one.Yet the pact's first real test is exposing how little Riyadh can actually count on Islamabad, whose army chief has far stronger incentives to stay out of a shooting war with Tehran than to jump into one on Saudi Arabia's behalf.Catch up quickSaudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement in September 2025 and expanded it into the three-way Mecca Pact in August 2026, with a joint secretariat based in Riyadh and Pakistan holding the first three-year chairmanship, Al Jazeera reported.The pact has never been invoked. Pakistan's defense minister, Khawaja Asif, said this week that an unprovoked attack on Saudi Arabia or a spillover of the Yemen war would make the Mecca agreement operational, adding, "there should be no doubt in this," though he gave no specifics on what that would look like in practice.Turkey's foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, has compared the pact's mechanics to NATO's, under which an attacked member requests specific help rather than triggering automatic intervention.There is not much clarity on when a Mecca pact member would seek help from others: Under what circumstance, an attack on a member would be regarded as an attack on all members?It is not clear whether Saudi Arabia has asked for Pakistan’s help in its fight against Houthis. As per an Axios report, MBS did reach out to US President Donald Trump to seek US help against Houthis. But Trump declined to come to Saudi Crown Prince’s rescue.Importantly, this isn't the first time Pakistan would be failing Saudi Arabia militarily. In 2015, Pakistan's parliament unanimously rejected King Salman's request to send troops into the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.Between the linesPakistan relies heavily on Saudi Arabia and the Gulf for foreign exchange, investment, energy support and financial assistance.That dependence cuts in Riyadh's favour on paper but works against a real Pakistani commitment in practice.As per reports, Pakistan already has roughly 16 JF-17 fighters, air-defense units and thousands of troops stationed in Saudi Arabia under earlier bilateral arrangements, which lets Munir point to a visible Pakistani footprint in the kingdom without ever having to fire a shot at the Houthis.But Munir has good reasons to hedge that have nothing to do with sentiment toward Riyadh. Pakistan shares a long, porous border with Iran and has its own security concerns there.Joining a campaign against the Houthis could turn Pakistan’s support for Riyadh into a confrontation with Iran and its partners.Pakistan also has a sizeable Shia population and may face domestic opposition if it intervenes directly in Saudi Arabia-Houthi fight.There's also a Washington dimension complicating things. Munir has spent the past year cultivating Donald Trump. With Trump having twice rejected Saudi requests for US strikes on the Houthis, Munir is unlikely to take a position that could put him at odds with the US president, especially on an issue where Trump has already made his position clear.There was not one air strike throughout the day (by Saudi support forces) ... It’s a Saudi-American f*** up of epic proportionsThe battlefield problemEven a willing Pakistan could not easily repair the military and political weaknesses exposed in Yemen. The Houthis’ advance was enabled partly by divisions among their opponents.Saudi-backed forces failed to cooperate effectively during the offensive. The withdrawal of the UAE also deprived the coalition of a capable supporter and deepened problems with southern factions.Additional Pakistani aircraft would not automatically resolve rival chains of command, competing territorial ambitions or distrust between local forces.Would Pakistan be defending Saudi airspace, reopening shipping lanes, recovering territory or helping impose a settlement? Each objective entails different resources and risks.The bottom line: MBS signed the Mecca Pact to buy himself military insurance against exactly the kind of Iranian-aligned assault now unfolding on his coastline.But Munir's incentives point toward mediating the Houthi crisis from Tehran's side of the table, not fighting it from Riyadh's, leaving Saudi Arabia's newest ally looking a lot more like a hedge than a rescue plan.(With inputs from agencies)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Built in 1975 and barely changed for 51 years, this 4,718-sq-ft shag-carpet Illinois home asked $259,900 and found a buyer within days
articles.summary: News News: Turns out, nostalgia is the buzzword in real estate these days. A house in East Dubuque, Illinois, was listed for $259,900, and in less than three day.
articles.body: Turns out, nostalgia is the buzzword in real estate these days. A house in East Dubuque, Illinois, was listed for $259,900, and in less than three days, many prospective buyers reached out. This 1975-built house didn't need a market rebound or a hot spring selling season to find buyers. People who understood its value came forward, and the new owner didn’t try to change anything. They want the house to be the way it was meant to be.Listing agent Olta Shabani of Equity Real Estate Group thinks the 4,718-sq-ft house is really frozen in time. “The owner passed away this summer [and] she built that house exactly the way she wanted to have it. All of her visions came to life back in 1975 when she built her dream house. It looks just like a complete time capsule,” Shabani told Realtor.com.When the colour palette became the main characterBuilt in 1975, the biggest highlight of this Illinois home is its bold colour choices. The three-bedroom and three-bathroom house is certainly not subtle and minimal like the homes we see today.Red dominates the huge lower level, which is the same size as the upper level at 4,718 sq ft. There is a red and black door, red kitchen cabinetry, and red curtains. “The basement has all red carpeting. The bar is really cool. There's a really nice wet bar area. There's also another kitchen area in the basement along with another bathroom, and it does walk out to the backyard,” Shabani told the outlet. The red sunken living room commands immediate attention, and the listing agent is obsessed with it. “My favourite thing is the sunken living room. It is just so massive and the stone fireplace there is really a focal point in that whole entire main level,” she added. The original owner of the house was really unapologetic about the colours.Green appears next, covering banisters and support poles and the wide solid stairs. Blue hues claimed the bedrooms.According to Shabani, this house is hands down one of the coolest houses in the area. It has the character that many houses down the street can only imagine. “It has always been known as the coolest house in the area,” she said. If the walls could talk, Shabani adds, “I think you would hear a lot of gatherings around the holidays. You would hear a lot of music. You would hear fun. I just could tell that this was a fun house.”Another unique design element of the house is the carpets. Thick and plush shag carpet runs through nearly every room, including the bathrooms. And that’s quite a deal, according to the listing agent. “The carpet is in excellent shape if your style is that thick shag carpeting. They don't make carpet today the way they used to back in the 70s, so it's in very, very good shape,” she said. There is, of course, a reason why carpets make a statement in this 1975 home. “It was in style, I guess, back in the day, and clearly it was quality because it lasted as long as it did.”Home finds its buyerWithin three days of being listed on the market, the home attracted buyers. The $259,900 home got a handful of prospective buyers. “I got offers within the first three days that we were on the market,” she said. But the agent wanted the home to find the right buyer. One who would really take pride in the home for what it is, rather than redecorating it to another aesthetic. “I really wanted to show in the pictures just the way that the house is. I didn't want to change anything. I didn't think it was appropriate for this type of house to virtually stage. I wanted people to see the character in it,” Shabani said.The sale closed with a buyer who recognised the distinction between preservation and museum curation. The buyer will retain the original character of the home while updating some fixtures and lighting. Not reimagining or erasing, only updating.“I know his main goal is to keep as much of the original character as possible while updating the things that would need to be updated right away, like fixtures and lighting and all that stuff.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Visa news: New Zealand launches 6-month work permit for international graduates from November 16. Who can apply?
articles.summary: Rest of World News: New Zealand will introduce a new work visa allowing eligible international graduates to work in the country for up to six months after completing thei.
articles.body: New Zealand will introduce a new work visa allowing eligible international graduates to work in the country for up to six months after completing their studies, with applications opening on November 16, 2026.The Short-Term Graduate Work Visa is designed for graduates who have completed eligible qualifications in New Zealand but do not qualify for the country's existing Post-Study Work Visa. Immigration New Zealand said the new route will give graduates time to find employment and potentially move to a longer-term work visa.The new visa will provide open work rights, meaning eligible holders can work for any employer in New Zealand. They do not need to have a job offer before applying.However, the visa is not available to every international student.Who is eligible?Applicants must have completed a New Zealand Qualifications and Credentials Framework (NZQCF) Level 5, 6 or 7 qualification in New Zealand.The qualification must have been studied full-time for at least 24 weeks in New Zealand and must not already make the graduate eligible for a Post-Study Work Visa. English-language, foundation and bridging qualifications are excluded.Applicants must also have at least NZ$5,000 available to support themselves during their stay and meet New Zealand's health and character requirements.There is also a strict application deadline. Graduates must apply within three months of the expiry of their New Zealand student visa.The visa can be granted only once. It cannot be extended or renewed.What happens after six months?The Short-Term Graduate Work Visa is intended as a bridge rather than a long-term post-study work route.During the six-month period, graduates can look for employment and, if eligible, move to another work visa such as New Zealand's Accredited Employer Work Visa.The new visa does not allow holders to own or operate a business. Work must be undertaken under an employment agreement or contract for services.New opportunity for graduates with bachelor's degreesAt the same time, New Zealand is expanding eligibility for its existing Post-Study Work Visa, a potentially much longer route.From November 16, graduates who complete an eligible Level 7 Graduate Diploma in New Zealand can qualify for a Post-Study Work Visa if they also hold a bachelor's degree.Importantly for international students, the bachelor's degree can be completed in New Zealand or overseas.This means, for example, that an Indian student who already has a bachelor's degree from India and completes an eligible Level 7 Graduate Diploma in New Zealand could qualify for the Post-Study Work Visa, provided all other requirements are met.The Graduate Diploma must be studied full-time in New Zealand for its entire duration. Cross-crediting or recognition of prior learning does not count towards the study requirement for this route.Post-study work visa can last up to 3 yearsThe existing Post-Study Work Visa remains the more extensive option for graduates who qualify.Depending on the qualification, it can allow graduates to stay and work in New Zealand for up to three years.Under the updated rules, eligible Level 8 postgraduate diploma graduates can receive up to one year of post-study work rights, while eligible master's graduates can receive up to three years, provided they meet the required full-time study conditions.The government said the changes are intended to strengthen New Zealand's international education sector while better aligning graduate pathways with the country's skills needs. For students planning to study in New Zealand, the choice of qualification will therefore be important: the new six-month visa is aimed at graduates who do not qualify for the longer Post-Study Work Visa, while certain higher-level qualifications can lead to substantially longer work rights.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the early 1970s, an American doctor travelled to India and spent time at Kainchi Dham; then Neem Karoli Baba called him "Doctor America" before his life changed forever
articles.summary: In the early 1970s, American physician Dr. Larry Brilliant travelled to India and spent time at Neem Karoli Baba’s ashram at Kainchi Dham, seeking spi.
articles.body: In the early 1970s, American physician Dr. Larry Brilliant travelled to India and spent time at Neem Karoli Baba’s ashram at Kainchi Dham, seeking spiritual guidance during a period of personal uncertainty. Baba reportedly began calling him “Doctor America”. In an interview with Tricycle: The Buddhist Review, he said the spiritual guru later urged him to go to Delhi and work for the United Nations to help eradicate smallpox.Brilliant eventually joined the World Health Organization’s smallpox eradication programme in India. His journey to the ashram and his work against the disease became closely connected in his later recollections. For Brilliant, the journey was deeply connected to his encounter with Neem Karoli Baba, whom he credited with giving his life a new direction.When he recalled his conversation with Neem Karoli BabaIn an interview published by Tricycle: The Buddhist Review in 2023, Dr. Larry Brilliant spoke about his time with Neem Karoli Baba and the teacher’s instruction to help eradicate smallpox. He said, “One day in July 1973, Neem Karoli Baba told me to go to Delhi immediately to work for the United Nations and help eradicate smallpox.” Brilliant recalled that the spiritual teacher had called him “Dr. America”.In the interview, he also spoke about the money he had with him and in America. “He (Neem Karoli Baba) said to me, Dr. America, because that was the name he had given me, Dr. America, how much money do you have? And that, you know, there's a whole other channel down which that goes. And I said, I have $500. He said, $500. You're lying. How much money do you have back in America?”Brilliant then thought about the time he had worked as an emergency room doctor. “And I said, I have $500 in America too.” The conversation soon turned into a joke, as Brilliant remembered it. “And then he started to chant. You have to understand that everything was funny. Everything was a comedian. Everything was a joke. He turned every single moment into something funnier than you ever thought anything could ever be.”Brilliant recalled Baba chanting about the money he had in India and the money he had in America. “And he started to chant $500 here, $500 there. You are no doctor, which is exactly what my mother had said to me. You can't make any money. You're not a real doctor.”He recalled that Baba continued repeating the words, first in Hindi and then in English. “$500 here, $500 there. You are no doctor. U-N-O doctor.” It was then that the conversation took a turn Brilliant would remember for the rest of his life.“United Nations organization. Dr. America is going to become a United Nations doctor. And you're going to work to help eradicate smallpox.” According to Brilliant’s recollection, Baba then spoke about the disease and its future. “Because this horrible disease is going to be lifted off of the back of humanity by God, who has a gift to humanity, will conquer this one form of suffering.”From Kainchi Dham to the fight against smallpoxBrilliant’s account of his encounter with Neem Karoli Baba is closely connected to his later work in public health. He eventually joined the World Health Organization’s smallpox eradication programme in India. The WHO campaign became one of the most significant achievements in global public health.In 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated worldwide. It was the first human disease to be officially declared eradicated. For Brilliant, the memory of Kainchi Dham remained connected to his professional journey. In his recollections, Neem Karoli Baba’s words gave him a new direction and encouraged him to use his medical skills in the fight against smallpox.Looking for trusted parenting advice?
